IR.rationale: REITs behave like long-duration, bond-like equities. A rise in intermediate yields relative to the policy rate raises discount rates and cap-rate expectations, which tends to weigh on subsequent REIT returns.

B.rationale: A credit sell-off (widening Baa spreads together with weak high-yield returns) signals a temporary rise in the price of risk. Leveraged real estate tends to earn this back afterwards through a higher expected return.

V.rationale: High equity implied volatility proxies a high variance risk premium and depressed prices, which predicts higher subsequent returns for risky assets.

AP.rationale: Strong recent market weeks tend to be partially reversed at short horizons. REITs also lag broad-market moves through their sector rotation.

ST.rationale: A strong conservative-minus-aggressive investment factor reflects rotation toward low-investment, income-oriented stocks, a style that REITs load on.

FX.rationale: Dollar strength reflects global risk and funding conditions. Domestically oriented REITs can benefit relatively when the dollar firms, so the sign is left for the model to learn.

COM.rationale: Silver rallies track falling real rates and rising inflation hedging demand. These moves in real-rate expectations tend to be reversed and feed into REIT pricing.

MC.rationale: Rising breakeven inflation pushes nominal yields up and raises discount rates, which pressures rate-sensitive REIT valuations over the following weeks.

ENDG.rationale: Weekly REIT returns show short-horizon mean reversion, so strong recent performance tends to be followed by weaker returns.

IR.rationale: Sharp falls in intermediate yields relative to the policy rate reflect flight-to-safety episodes and repricing of the policy outlook. Such moves precede higher realised volatility in risky assets.

B.rationale: Weak high-yield returns together with widening Baa spreads mark credit stress. Credit stress raises the volatility of leveraged real-estate equity beyond what its own past variance implies.

V.rationale: Implied volatility is forward-looking and contains information about future realised variance not captured by trailing realised variance.

AP.rationale: A joint US and EM equity sell-off signals a global risk-off shock. Through the leverage effect and volatility feedback, it raises subsequent volatility.

ST.rationale: Outperformance of profitable firms reflects a flight to quality that typically accompanies rising uncertainty.

FX.rationale: Broad dollar strength combined with yen appreciation is the classic safe-haven, carry-unwind pattern of risk-off episodes, which precede higher realised volatility.

COM.rationale: Broad commodity declines signal weakening global demand and risk-off conditions that tend to raise cross-asset volatility.

MC.rationale: Tight financial conditions raise funding costs and constrain intermediaries. This amplifies price swings in leveraged, financing-dependent sectors such as REITs.

ENDG.rationale: High recent realised variance may partially mean-revert relative to the baseline volatility model, so its level carries residual information.

IR.rationale: Bear steepening driven by rising long yields raises the long-duration discount rates that matter most for REIT valuations, increasing the risk of a sharp drawdown.

B.rationale: Widening Baa spreads raise the cost of debt refinancing for leveraged property owners and signal deteriorating credit, which fattens the left tail.

V.rationale: Elevated equity and gold implied volatility together indicate broad macro uncertainty, including about real rates. This raises the probability of extreme outcomes.

AP.rationale: Small-cap underperformance indicates tightening risk appetite and funding for smaller, more leveraged firms, a profile shared by many REITs.

ST.rationale: A flight to profitable, high-quality firms accompanies risk-off phases in which leveraged sectors face larger downside tails.

FX.rationale: A rapidly strengthening dollar tightens global financial conditions and is associated with risk-off episodes.

COM.rationale: Precious-metal rallies reflect hedging demand and inflation or real-rate repricing, which can precede sharp moves in rate-sensitive assets.

MC.rationale: Tight financial conditions raise the likelihood of forced deleveraging and large losses in credit-dependent real estate.

ENDG.rationale: Recent weak returns raise volatility through the leverage effect and can trigger further selling, increasing the chance of an extreme loss.

IR.rationale: Falling intermediate yields relative to the policy rate lower discount rates and favour bond-proxy REITs, raising the chance of a strong rally.

B.rationale: After credit spreads have widened, risk premia are elevated, and relief rallies in leveraged real estate become more likely.

V.rationale: High implied volatility widens the return distribution and coincides with depressed prices, so both tails, including large rebounds, become more likely.

AP.rationale: Weak recent market returns tend to be followed by short-horizon rebounds, raising the probability of a large gain.

ST.rationale: Strong performance of conservative, low-investment stocks signals rotation toward income-oriented equities like REITs.

FX.rationale: Yen appreciation accompanies falling global yields and risk-off phases that precede rate-driven REIT rebounds.

COM.rationale: Commodity weakness lowers inflation and yield pressure, a backdrop for strong rallies in rate-sensitive assets.

MC.rationale: Elevated financial stress widens the return distribution. Stress episodes are followed by sharp relief rallies once conditions ease.

ENDG.rationale: Short-horizon mean reversion makes large gains more likely after weak recent REIT performance.
